TLDR;  Devs won't add blocks the community has been asking for (for years).  Complexity limit is fixed unless modded.  No control settings unless you change them for EVERY build you create.

This game is about building, yet the devs refuse to add basic blocks, for instance there is no 1x1x1 block.  SEVERAL blocks that should exist simply don't, there are slopes with matching corner pieces and slopes without matching corner pieces.  There is no consistency in the availability of blocks.  This fact has also become a meme of sorts as the devs have acted in the past as though they had intentions to change these things and yet never have.  The devs have even said that adding those parts would "alter the game play experience" and make building too easy, however I have to disagree with this.  If you have an idea in your head and the only reason you can't build it or have to find some work around is the lack of a block the devs have neglected to add to "make the game harder", it's hard to enjoy your "game play experience", and leads me to turn the game off.  I have hundreds of hours in this game when it very well could be thousands.  Limit blocks from certain game modes, yes, but don't neglect to add them into the game at all.  Lack of freedom is why I never stick around long.

Your build is limited to a certain complexity as if you're playing on console.  Every ones PC is different in some way, complexity should be available in the settings menu for single player and server menu for multiplayer.  A mod should not be required.  Every game I start I load up the mod (thus opting out of high scores and subsequently a large portion of the "game play experience") and set my complexity to 2000, I have never had a single issue and I have had to turn it up on occasion.  My "game play experience" is 30 to 60 seconds in a UI every time I load into a world.

Default controls can not be set.  If you place an engine, it will be mapped to W/S, place a thruster, maps to space.  This should be configurable in the settings.  It's a waste of build time when certain things you place ALWAYS get mapped to certain buttons and you ALWAYS have to change them because you can't change the defaults.  It's to the point I'd almost be happier if everything spawned in unmapped, at least then when I didn't want something mapped I could just not open it, rather than opening the settings and clearing the default mapping that would have been incorrect for me had I even wanted it mapped.

Not to mention the recent release of High Seas which feels more like a tech demo than proper DLC.  I love this game, but have little faith in the devs, and thus, the games future.

After spending quite a bit of time with Trailmakers, I can honestly say that it is a fun game, but it's also one of the most frustrating games I've played when it comes to wasted potential.

My biggest issue is the lack of variety in the base game's building blocks. For a game that revolves entirely around creativity and engineering, the selection of wedges, corner wedges, and aircraft panels feels surprisingly limited. I constantly find myself unable to build what I envision because a simple structural piece doesn't exist unless I buy another DLC.

That leads into what I consider the game's biggest problem: monetization. The base game may cost around $24, but if you actually want access to many of the useful or interesting blocks, the price quickly climbs well beyond $100. I recently bought a $20 DLC almost exclusively for a single block I needed for a build, and that felt ridiculous. Paying for additional campaigns or cosmetic content is one thing, but paying for basic building pieces in a sandbox game feels more like being nickel-and-dimed than supported with expansions.

Multiplayer has also been a disappointment in my experience. Public servers are often laggy, physics can become unstable, and larger creations only make these problems worse. A game built around showing off creations and playing with others loses a lot of its appeal when multiplayer struggles to function smoothly.

Another frustration is that the game often feels neglected. There are building limitations and quality-of-life issues that have existed for a long time, yet new DLC continues to appear while many of the core problems remain. It creates the impression that selling more content takes priority over improving the foundation of the game itself.

Even with all of that, I still find myself coming back to Trailmakers. The vehicle-building system is genuinely enjoyable, and when everything works, the game can be incredibly fun. That's what makes these issues so disappointing. The game has the potential to be one of the best sandbox builders available, but in its current state it feels like that potential is being held back by expensive DLC, neglected features, and technical problems.

I'm leaving a negative review not to demote the game and leave potential buyers on edge about purchasing it, but more to make you guys reading this aware of what is to come.

At the time of writing, Trailmakers is a sandbox and construction game that perfectly knows its mission statement and sticks by it: it's a game about constructing vehicles - things that get you or your stuff from Point A to Point B by definition - and extrapolating every possible, reasonable gameplay conclusion from that. 
You get a campaign mode that flavors this as a progressive puzzle game, where you construct vehicles as creative solutions to get to hidden parts and treasures in obscure areas and figure out how to take it back to a collection point, no matter how big, round, or explosive it is.

You get several racing game modes, some giving you limited part budgets to construct the best possible racing car, plane, boat, or other thing, to get through the course as quickly as possible. Others provide less restrictions on what's expected of you, just so long as you have wheels. And others yet are just an all-out muscle test of how fast you can clear a completely smooth half-pipe loop, without your vehicle exploding from sheer G-forces.

This all stems from a construction set and UI that allows you to build these machines up to precise specifications, expecting a degree of understanding from the player of how principles of physics such as drag, center of mass, axle distances, center of thrust and lift, and even logic-gating, can be leveraged to create anything ranging from standard-grade cars, boats, and planes - to the outright outlandish, even providing you with special tools like magnets to pick up objects (or other vehicles!) cannons, and terrain anchors (literally making your creation immobile) to make cranes, tanks, and even stationary buildings, rides, or emplacements for the hell of it.

This is the heart of the game, and Flashbulb did their best to make it fun and simple to use, to the ends of making 3 separate sandbox maps that each emphasize their own approaches (one for exploration, one for utter mayhem and destruction, and one for pure control-environment prototyping).

And even if you don't have a PhD in physics, don't worry, because the actual goal-oriented aspects of Trailmakers (races and campaign) are completely viable to complete without having to ever use anything aside from blueprints the game gives you by default - maybe a couple of tweaks here and there for control preferences or additional capacity, but other than that, it gives you plenty of leeway to work on these as templates.

It doesn't try to convolute itself with notions of traditional approaches that games like this can take towards ideas of survival, or combat, or head-to-head multiplayer battles, or anything similar. The options and tools for those are theoretically there, but it's not ever the core conceit of any of the game modes; it's not the point.

It is a game about building vehicles, and to this end, it's achieved precisely what it needed to for that.

This is the kind of game where you are given a massive selection of various blocks, motorized parts, wheels, etc. and are told "go wild". The only limitation to what kind of machines you create are your imagination and whether or not you can make them work. And trust me, if you're willing to tinker and hone your design enough you CAN make it work. There are people who have literally made fully functional DOOM arcade machines, it's insane what you can achieve. Want to build a submarine that can hover on land and transforms into a helicopter? Absolutely. Wanna make a pickup truck that can fly in space? Yes sir, it's actually fairly easy to do. Want a realistic CIWS automated defense system complete with on-board laser targeting system? Believe it or not, YES.

Gameplay aside, I really like how active the developers are with their community. Frequent build challenges give the players a chance to show off their best work (and even a chance to be featured in the main menu as background footage!) and dev vlogs show off upcoming content, allowing players to see the new parts in action, get technical info about them, etc. Furthermore, features that get highly requested will often make it into the game, provided the team doesn't hit a roadblock with technical limitations. For example, the community has wanted tank tracks for YEARS, and it took the team 5 tries over the years to add them and they had to LITERALLY reinvent the wheel to make it happen, but make it happen they did. I'm not joking by the way, they had to rebuild the wheel system from the ground up to add them, and every wheel in the game benefited from it. But, here's that technical limitation I mentioned: people wanted *modular* tracks, but unfortunately the build menu can't do that, blocks have no way of linking up to each other like that. Each segment of the track would be its own block, which could cause problems on bigger builds. Just don't ask for a 1x1x1 cube. They staunchly refuse to add it.

Now, the game isn't perfect, so I do want to mention this:
They do often release DLC. Sometimes it might just be a few blocks and some cosmetics, other times it might just be player outfits, and sometimes it's an entire map/campaign. The game itself has a nice lineup of sandbox maps as well as 2 "campaigns", so to speak. Stranded is the much older of the 2, and is fairly simple in its style: You have a limited array of parts to build a vehicle with and you have to collect various scrap chunks and bring them to checkpoints to unlock new parts and eventually build an escape rocket to get home. No enemies, no mission system, just the challenge of collecting things in increasingly difficult locations.

Pioneers is the much newer one, and it is an ACTUAL campaign: unlock blocks through finding crates, harvest materials to actually CRAFT the blocks and increase the amount of them in your inventory (Stranded doesn't use this, you just have infinite uses of a block on any given build), and combat the robotic mining mega-corp BOTNAK as they ravage the area for resources.

There are also 2 other campaigns and a collectible-littered sandbox map in the major DLC: High Seas, an aquatic map with wind and various intensity of waves, from relaxed swells to LITERAL ACTUAL TSUNAMIS; Airborne, battling against mostly aerial space pirates; and Frozen Tracks, bringing the battle back to the BOTNAK to, once again, stop them from decimating a planet in their never-ending lust for material gain.

Now, some people may not take kindly to this approach because "drowning in DLC RAAAAHHHHHH", and while I do think some of the smaller packs like Space Voyager should've just been built-in, I also recognize that they have to make money *somehow* and this game isn't exactly a mainstream AAA title so it's not like they have some massive publisher sending them truckloads of cash on a daily basis, you gotta do what you gotta do. 

In my opinion, they've earned my support because they've worked closely with their community to make an amazing game for those who have a creative itch and I'm excited to see what the next update will hold.

After spending nearly 1000 hrs of my life into the game (and now that I'm typing it, it's kind of scary), I can firmly guarantee that I've never played a vehicles related game that has let me express my creativity this much.

What to expect:

The racing experience - Splitted between Rally Mode and the various races across Race Island, it allows you to get the necessary experience in terms of driving (but mostly in terms of building), in order to understand the way the aerodynamics and the physics works in the game, of course providing also a lot of fun and ingame currency to unlock more and more parts. You will race with any sort of things, including airplanes, hovercrafts, hydrofoils (wait hydrofoils? Yep), boats, submarines, not only cars.

The replica experience - After a while, you will see replicas of a large number of vehicles around the workshop, and you'll start craving to build one of them. Your favourite Jet? Your favourite tank? Your favourite car? Your own car?? Recreating them is a proper challenge in terms of realism, but the fun and the amount of satisfaction at the end of the process is guaranteed.

Multiplayer - You've got a bunch of mates that are trying to fine tuning their race cars to climb the leaderboards right? Create (host) a server, invite them, and instead of helping them, spawn your favourite tank and start shooting them!! Racecars always provides a nice challenge as targets. Don't you worry, they'll just have to press R to quickly respawn. Just hope they don't decide to spawn their favourite jet bomber instead :D

The Workshop - Trying others ideas kindly shared in the workshop it's always nice, isn't it? Just don't reupload stuff that does not belong to you, it's just a D move and you'll get reported. Just saying.

The Community - The devs runs a Community Discord, I can say it's a nice crowded place. There you'll find any sorts of stuff: blueprints, crazy gifs & screenshots, building tips and ideas, weekly challenges, and u'll get support from both players and devs. Just be polite.

Sure the game is fun and enjoyable, and there's no singular thing wrong with it to ruin the experience, but there are *a lot* of small and/or minor things which all add up into a lack of polish.

Most of these things aren't gameplay blockers or major annoyances, so I still can recommend it, but there are just *so many* small things adding up that I never had a chance to forget about the problems, such as:

- Unexplained deaths and/or vehicle damage: for the most part the game is quite forgiving and you don't often take 'accidental' damage, but when you do it is always severe and unintuitive or unexplained
- Unreliable part controls: putting multiple parts working together or using them in a way the game didn't expect can often lead to controls simply not working, or very weird behavior that doesn't make sense. I found myself having to *delete and re-build* and re-configure the part controls to fix it in some cases.
- Obviously wrong physics behaviors: in multiple occasions I have had situations where the physics simply break down, such as the main chassis of a solid vehicle splitting in half and rotating *instead of* the turret on the aiming servo, which somehow remains still???
- Missing keybindings and controls options: in a game all about configuring your own vehicle and the way it works, and in every other game I've seen of the genre, I expect to have simple things like being able to bind extra mouse buttons (4/5, forward and back, etc) or reconfigure all of the game's own controls.

Luckily, none of these issues were major enough to stop me from enjoying the game, so I can still click 'Yes' for Steam, but I really hope that the devs will spend some time cleaning up the edge cases and making the foundation of the game rock-solid before moving on to adding fanciful new campaigns or content.

Trailmakers is an entertaining building game. There is a sandbox mode, but the real fun is the campaign. The main campaign has you crash landed on a alien planet. The pieces of your ship and cargo are now scattered all over the planet. In order to escape, you must find all the salvage and use these pieces to ultimately build a rocket ship to escape. 

There's virtually no story, the planet is quite lifeless and mostly unremarkable. What's fun, however, is finding and using the salvage scattered around the planet to build all sorts of devices to help you achieve your goal. You'll start with a simple car but as you get more pieces, you'll end up building more complicated and fanciful machines. By the end, I built a monster truck and floats on water with a retractable tractor beam arm, a hover ship (multiple versions that got better over time) that helped me fly into a volcano and retrieve a critical piece of salvage, and a submarine to explore the deep tranches for loot. It was a blast. And you'll need to be really creative because some of the salvage can be deviously hard to get to and bring back to your salvage nodes. 

The game gives you templates to build some basic crafts, but the real fun is building your own. The sky's the limit because you're given a large array of blocks and tools to make just the right machine for the job. 

I played the entire game with a controller and it worked pretty well, which surprised me as games like this are usually MK only. The game also ran very smooth even with complicated machines. There is also a lot of game packed in, with different campaigns, modes, and a previously mentioned sandbox mode. You will absolutely get your money's worth.

I was a bit apprehensive at first as I was afraid the game would have a steep learning curve like many sandbox games do. But it doesn’t, really. It does a wonderful job at introducing you gradually to its features. Building something that does the job you need it to do is quite easy.

On top of that, the game’s very well optimized and polished. Performance and stability is not an issue (as much as you can expect of a sandbox game, mind you).

That’s a result of the game having a few years on it by this point, but make no mistake, this is NOT another dead game. It receives frequent updates that add new building blocks and features, refine the user interface, increase stability and performance. As such, you can always find servers to play with others.

The devs clearly listen to their community. They’ve added plenty of features that we’ve been asking for. In fact, they do community surveys. Everyone wanted tank tracks. Guess what’s coming in the next update?
It might not have the depth of Stormworks or the crazy versatility of Garry’s Mod. But Trailmakers doesn’t require days or weeks of work for a single vehicle. It’s far more refined than Garry’s Mod and won’t break your spirit while building complex stuff.

And trust me, you can get as simple and as complex as you want. You can slap a seat, some wheels and an engine and you got yourself a vehicle. But there’s logic stuff so if you feel like programming a whole game cabinet to recreate Mario in-game, you can.
